edges.label: Subgroups and markers

edges.label: Tracing and intervention
edges.evidence: Mouse Ctsk genetic labeling and injury/function experiments support that periosteal populations participate in bone formation and repair.
edges.limit: Functional experiments summarized involve the Ctsk driving range; it does not equal specific manipulation of the Ctsk∩Ly6a double-positive population.

edges.label: Regional comparison
edges.evidence: Original research records and abstracts comparing Gli1-labeled cells in different regions of the mandible.
edges.limit: Co-labeling cannot prove the same functional group; the specific induction window still needs to be checked in the full text.

edges.label: Comparison of offspring
edges.evidence: Comparison of offspring with induced genetic tracing and tissue supports differences in output between regions.
edges.limit: This is a regional comparison; it cannot be used to establish upstream and downstream relationships of all periosteal labeled populations.

studies.clinical: Suggests that recovery strategies need to consider regions; therapeutic effects have not been evaluated.

studies.headline: Identify IFITM5 populations on the surface of human fetal bone, then use functional experiments to define capability.

edges.label: Functional testing
edges.evidence: The authors connect single-cell, spatial sampling, and tissue localization with sorting, clonal culture, and transplantation.
edges.limit: Atlas type and functional cell definition are two layers of evidence; this is not continuous embryonic to adult tracing.

edges.label: Experimental output
edges.evidence: Clonal culture and transplantation support the self-renewal and biased osteogenic capacity of the studied populations.
edges.limit: Adult experiments come from bone fragments and cultured BMSC; not all stages can be assigned to the same outer periosteum location.

studies.clinical: Support cell capability; patient repair efficacy is not proven.

frameworks.name: Origin and positional identity
frameworks.short: Where it comes from and where it forms
frameworks.question: Where do the cells come from? Why does this location form specific jaw structures?
frameworks.claim: Sources provide context; intrinsic cellular programs and local signals together participate in positional identity, size, and developmental timing.
claims: Neural crest or mesoderm origins are a different issue from adult cell types.
The same source can form different tissues; positional patterns and species-specific morphology also need separate explanations.
frameworks.unknown: Which morphological features depend on the cell's own program, and which require a specific host environment?
frameworks.boundary: Bird transplantation and mouse tracing each have their scope and cannot replace the complete lineage of the human mandible. Same source does not mean the local cells are the same.

clinical.problem: Congenital structural identity or morphological abnormalities
clinical.question: Does early positioning abnormality occur when cells arrive, at position specification, or during subsequent tissue formation?
clinical.limit: These are research evaluation suggestions; the source mechanism itself is not evidence for therapy.

frameworks.name: Regional tissue formation
frameworks.short: Why does this tissue form here
frameworks.question: Why does the same mesenchyme form bone, cartilage, tendon and non-mineralized interfaces in different regions?
frameworks.claim: Tissue fate, local environment, and boundaries need to be explained regionally; one marker or one ossification method cannot generalize the entire jaw.
claims: Different segments of Meckel's cartilage can undertake different tasks.
Local maps, lineage contributions, and tissue boundaries complement each other and cannot replace one another.
frameworks.unknown: When is regional identity established, and which boundaries can change with load or injury?
frameworks.boundary: Ossification methods describe tissue processes or spatial relationships and do not automatically equal independent cell lineages. New author models also do not automatically become field consensus.

clinical.problem: Local growth deficiency or interface tissue imbalance
clinical.question: First determine which segment, which tissue, and which boundary are lacking, then choose the matching cell or tissue endpoint.
clinical.limit: Enhanced osteogenesis does not necessarily improve regional morphology or non-mineralized interfaces.

frameworks.name: Tissue coordination and attachment
frameworks.short: How to assemble a functional musculoskeletal system
frameworks.question: How do bone, cartilage, tendon, and muscle from different sources connect in the correct position and timing?
frameworks.claim: While different tissues are forming, connections must also be established in the correct location and timing; local signals, matrix tissue, and mechanical transmission can each participate synergistically.
claims: The origins of muscle and connective tissue can be different, yet they need to form connections together.
The initiation, recruitment, and maintenance of tendons, as well as attachment maturation, are different processes.
frameworks.unknown: Do changes in mandibular morphology come from the tendon's own fate, nearby signals, or altered force transmission?
frameworks.boundary: Embryonic co-development abnormalities cannot be directly treated as isolated causal evidence of postnatal masticatory load. Conclusions from limbs or birds need verification for applicability to the jaw.

clinical.problem: Tendon or attachment abnormalities, insufficient connection after reconstruction
clinical.question: Evaluate bone morphology, attachment location, transitional tissue, and muscle function simultaneously to determine which link the functional disorder occurs in.
clinical.limit: Tissue adjacency, imaging proximity, or fiber connections do not necessarily equal normal mature attachment.

frameworks.name: Functional growth adaptation
frameworks.short: How movement and load feedback onto growth
frameworks.question: How function, local forces, and tissue remodeling jointly alter size, shape, and spatial position.
frameworks.claim: Structure affects load, and load also affects tissue; early forces within cells and tissues should be separated from later mastication and external loads.
claims: Local bone formation/resorption and displacement of the whole bone occur at different scales.
The same load change may produce different results in different regions.
frameworks.unknown: Who generates the force, how it is transmitted, which cells receive it, and which function is ultimately changed?
frameworks.boundary: Moss’s 1997 revision combines genetic and non-genetic factors. Classic morphologic rules do not equal cellular mechanisms; load experiments in one part cannot define all mandibular growth.

clinical.problem: Imbalance of growth due to disuse, abnormal load, or susceptible joints
clinical.question: Link load conditions with local tissue responses, morphology improvement, and functional recovery segment by segment.
clinical.limit: Changes in soft food or disuse models do not automatically constitute intervention schemes applicable to all patients.

frameworks.name: Homeostasis and repair
frameworks.short: How to restore structure and function after damage
frameworks.question: Which local cells respond after damage? How to simultaneously restore tissue, connections, and function?
frameworks.claim: Repair depends on local cells and their environment; The potential and expression state after injury cannot be directly considered a normal developmental lineage.
claims: The periosteum, bone marrow, and attachment interface show different responses and tissue output.
Bone mass, tissue quality, connections, and function are different recovery endpoints.
frameworks.unknown: Can increased cellular contribution bring lasting structural and functional improvements? What reversible steps are available after developmental abnormalities form?
frameworks.boundary: Development does not equal injury repair. In vitro differentiation, animal healing, and patient benefit must be verified separately.

clinical.problem: Bone defects, attachment injuries, and insufficient functional reconstruction
clinical.question: First identify the disease and functional defects, then examine local cellular and causal mechanisms, and systemic recovery after intervention.
clinical.limit: Early cases, animal or cell rescues, each supporting different degrees of conclusion, cannot be combined into a cured disease.

alveolar.text: Local progenitor identity and load response are two separate issues; alveolar bone results cannot represent the entire mandible.

condyle.text: First distinguish perichondrium, cartilage, bone, and attachment areas, then determine which aspects are improved by growth, load reduction, or reconstruction.

subchondral.text: Local osteogenic regulation, contribution of cartilage descendants, and fracture response need to be verified separately.

coronoid.text: Initial establishment of the coronoid process is connected to subsequent temporalis-related growth, but it is not the same process.

masseter.text: Three research lines consist of embryonic co-occurrence, postnatal load, and attachment repair; they cannot be combined into a single traction mechanism.

angle.text: Interface fate, tendon connection, and load output are interrelated; bone reconstruction still requires evaluation of attachment and function.

periosteum.text: Periosteal origin, local populations, and repair outcomes need to be identified separately; stiffness behavior cannot substitute for healing or morphological recovery.

marrow.text: Position, age, and induction timing change tissue contribution; perivascular markers do not equal muscle origin.

arch.text: Source, spatial specification, and cell rearrangement jointly organize early tissue structure; endogenous cell force should be interpreted on a functional scale.

meckel.text: Distinguish stepwise cell descendants, local signals, and temporary scaffolds; do not depict the entire cartilage as a uniform osteogenic lineage.

ossification.text: Osteogenic maps, origin, and local cartilage effects are complementary evidence and cannot be combined into an unverified continuous lineage.

embtendon.text: Tendon initiation, maintenance, and formation of different attachments need to be read according to region and timing.

palate.text: Maxilla and palate are used to compare regional fate and microenvironment and do not serve as direct evidence for mandible localization.

calvaria.text: Use cranial suture niches and functional validation as a reference, preserving tissue origin and positional differences.

longbone.text: Long bones provide reference for periosteal layering and post-injury mobilization and cannot directly define the same-named cells in the jaw.

enthesis.text: Limb attachment occurrence, load, and regeneration are used for problem comparison; structure and weight-bearing function are evaluated separately.

reviews.text: Reviews help address tissue issues; author theories, research routes, and page synthesis need to be marked separately.

cranialcompare.text: Birds and fish help separate source, partition, and connection mechanisms; species and tissue differences are prerequisites for extrapolation.

paper-data.institution: Peking University School of Stomatology

paper-data.cells: Postoperative masticatory muscles and bone connections; muscle volume
paper-data.framework: Mandibular morphology reconstruction and restoration of muscle connections are not the same
paper-data.claim: Among 30 patients aged 7–68 years, lateral pterygoid reattachment in 25 cases; masseter reattachment in 3 cases, 27 cases of ectopic attachment, medial pterygoid all ectopic attachment. New condyle regeneration occurred in 16 cases, all accompanied by lateral pterygoid reattachment; regeneration was more common in younger patients.
paper-data.boundary: CT determines the connection morphology but cannot confirm tendon-bone tissue quality; the article reports that the entire group could open their mouths and eat solids, but did not perform quantitative functional comparison based on reattachment. labels.scope: Current focus: local cell populations, periosteum, condyle and tendon–muscle–bone interactions; other topics remain partial.
labels.scopeBody: This is a focused reading map assembled through Chinese- and English-language topic searches, paper reading and citation tracking. This revision checks bibliography and selected results using PubMed/Europe PMC, Crossref and journal sources. No preregistered systematic-review search or duplicate screening was performed.
labels.scopeGaps: Dental–periodontal, neurovascular, immune and some repair topics remain incompletely covered. Few entries indicate limited map coverage, not absence of research. Comparative tissues and theory sources are labeled separately.
labels.inventory: 96 main records plus 7 framework sources: 103 independent references; 2 preprints hidden by default.
labels.sortRecommended: Suggested reading order follows this region’s questions; it is not an evidence ranking.
labels.sortYear: Newest first; ties ordered by ID.
labels.unitOnly: The assessments below apply to linked experiments, not the entire paper.
labels.notComparable: A shared marker or nearby site does not establish direct comparability; check models and endpoints first.
